newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Media moguls Murdoch and Packer settle litigation.
newsitem.headline: Media moguls Murdoch and Packer settle litigation.

text.p: Media rivals Rupert Murdoch and Kerry Packer settled all legal claims between their business interests on Thursday, heading off what promised to be a bitter court battle over film and television rights.

Lachlan Murdoch, managing director of his father's Australian operations, said litigation on all claims between Packer's Nine Network Australia and News Ltd, News Corp Ltd's Australian unit, had been settled on undisclosed terms.

The two companies were due in court later this year over a claim by Nine Network that News had breached an agreement to provide it with exclusive access to products from News' Twentieth Century Fox film and television division.

The dispute over the supply of Fox programming came while News Ltd's Super League was battling with the Australian Rugby League (ARL), backed by Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd (PBL) chief Kerry Packer, for control of rugby league.

"This removes the final impediment between Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd and News Ltd in relation to Super League and allows us to concentrate on what we both do best," Murdoch said in a brief statement.
News and PBL also announced that Packer's Channel Nine had won the free-to-air broadcast rights for Monday night Super League matches.
Nine already holds the free-to-air rights for ARL matches.
"This deal does not in any way alter the Nine Network's existing contract with the ARL," PBL managing director James Packer, son of Australia's richest man, said in a statement.

"We also believe that the Nine Network telecasting both ARL and Super League will increase the prospect of a unified rugby league competition which, we believe, to be in the best interests of the public, viewers and all parties," Packer said.
Super League matches will be shown on the pay-television network Foxtel, owned jointly by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp and government-owned telecommunications group Telstra.
Foxtel's rival Optus Vision owns the pay-television rights to ARL matches. Optus was one of the ARL's major backers during the protracted and often bitter dispute with Super League.

Super League, an important part of Murdoch's global sports-driven pay-television network, won a major victory over the ARL last October when Australia's Federal Court ruled Murdoch's rugby league competition could begin next year.

Super League had appealed against an earlier ruling banning the rebel competition from starting before 2000. News Ltd invested A$270 million (US$210 million) in its two-year battle with the ARL, the game's traditional rulers in Australia.
ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker told reporters he was disappointed by the deal between News Ltd and Channel Nine but said it did not signal a compromise between the two sides.
"Reading any more into it is just fuelling speculation," Whittaker said.
"Of course we're disappointed but it's done. At least we now know whereabouts and when Super League will be on television." (A$1 = US$0.78)
